reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes Hashflare cloud-mining contracts through a referral URL, showing paid one-year Equihash options and a purchase process. It ties a claimed return of more than 200% per year to the same Zcash contract purchase, although the evidence does not establish that the returns were achieved or guaranteed.

opening.argument: Judge, the speaker's return figure should be read alongside his explicit uncertainty, not as a promise. He says, "Yesterday it could have cost me $0.90 Today it might have cost me $0.5" and "nobody knows what the money will make". The screen also qualifies the stated November date as approximate. Those qualifications leave room for an overoptimistic opinion about a volatile opportunity, but they do not establish that viewers were promised a fixed payout.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited annual-return figure is a claim, not evidence of a guaranteed or achieved payout. The speaker also acknowledges that the value might change and that its future is unknown. Nor does the referral URL, by itself, turn that uncertain forecast into a promise to viewers.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Uncertainty about future value does not neutralize the pitch for a paid mining contract. The speaker reports completing a purchase and immediately presents its returns as "more than 200%" per year, while the description supplies a referral link. The concern is that promotional combination, not proof that a payout was guaranteed or achieved.

opening.argument: Judge, the video can be understood as a first-person walkthrough of a mining interface. The speaker begins by discussing what Zcash is, then identifies a contract option, selects payment from his own balance, and reports the purchase result. The visible interface shows the hashpower selection rather than a payout. That sequence demonstrates how this particular contract is selected and bought; it does not show an instruction that viewers must buy it or evidence that anyone earned the stated return.

rebuttal.rebuttal: A completed purchase can be part of a demonstration. The quoted confirmation establishes what the speaker says happened in his session, not that viewers were instructed to purchase. Likewise, the interface selection establishes a price and quantity on screen, not actual mining proceeds or a guaranteed result.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A walkthrough can still promote the transaction it demonstrates. Here the speaker urges buying, reports a successful purchase, and associates the Zcash contract with a claimed annual return above 200%. The referral link gives viewers a route to the same service. No verified proceeds are needed to recognize the paid-mining return pitch.

opening.argument: Judge, the concrete transaction shown is a priced cloud-mining service: the speaker describes a small hashpower purchase and says he paid from his balance. The description includes a service link, but the supplied material does not show a credential request, downline-income arrangement, or a guaranteed payout. A referral link and a purchase, without those further elements, can also describe ordinary promotion of a service; this record does not establish that the service failed to deliver what was bought.

But its own evidence does not establish a guaranteed payment or show that the described purchase produced no mining service. The visible interface shows a selection and zero current hashpower; it is not evidence of a realized return either way.

The speaker presents a paid hashpower purchase, gives viewers a referral URL, and claims returns exceeding 200% per year for the Zcash contract. The material does not verify that return. Calling the transaction ordinary commerce does not account for how the return claim is used to promote it.
